messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

María is a 30-year-old bank teller who has been married for four years. She sought therapy after months of escalating distress that she could no longer manage on her own. The traumatic event occurred two years ago, when she was abducted from a parking garage after a late shift. Over the course of three days, she was held captive and tortured by a group of men who took turns watching her, their faces sometimes calm as they inflicted pain, their voices rising in anger when she struggled. She remembers the silence between their words—long, heavy pauses that made the next blow feel inevitable. When she was finally released, she told no one the full extent of what happened, believing it was safer to bury the memory.

The memory, however, has never stayed buried. It returns without warning—a sudden shift in her surroundings can bring it back completely across all her senses: the smell of the garage, the pressure of a hand on her shoulder, the cold tile floor against her back. When this happens, she feels so overwhelmed by emotion that she has to stop whatever she is doing, frozen in the past while the present dissolves. These intrusions have become more frequent over time, and she has noticed that they are often triggered by specific cues: a customer expressing frustration at her window, even calmly, can send her heart racing; the sensation of being watched while she counts cash makes her palms sweat. Sexual situations with her husband have become nearly impossible—she tenses at his touch, her mind catapulting back to the hands that held her down. She has come to believe that any expression of anger in others signals imminent danger, and she scans every face that enters the bank for signs of irritation, her body bracing for an attack.

This sense of threat has become a constant companion. She startles at the slightest unexpected sound—a drawer slamming, a phone ringing—and she wakes during the night to check whether she is safe, listening to the silence of the apartment with a certainty that something terrible is about to happen. Unusual silence itself feels dangerous now, a prelude to violence. The more hypervigilant she becomes, the more the memory surfaces; her own alertness seems to summon it, as though her body is proving to her mind that the danger is still present. She has tried to cope by going over and over the details of the event, replaying each moment in an attempt to make sense of why it happened and how she could have prevented it. This rumination, however, only sharpens the memory, making the next intrusion more vivid. She finds herself spending money impulsively on clothes and electronics she does not need, a brief distraction that leaves her feeling emptier and more exposed, as though she has drawn attention to herself. She avoids eye contact with customers and colleagues, certain that if someone meets her gaze they will see her fear and know she is weak, which will invite further harm. Her husband has noticed her pulling away, though she cannot explain why; she has told him only that she feels anxious, not that his quiet presence in bed sometimes feels like the silence before a blow.

The causal loops have tightened into a cycle she cannot escape. A customer’s raised voice triggers a surge of threat, which sends her into a replay of the event, which drives her to ruminate or buy something online, which leaves her more vigilant the next day. She has started calling in sick once a week, afraid that the bank—once a place of routine—has become a minefield of cues. What finally brought her to therapy was a morning when she saw her husband’s face in the bathroom mirror as he asked if she was okay, and for a split second she did not recognize him as safe. She is most afraid that the memory will never stop feeling real, and she is hoping—though she does not quite believe it—that someone can teach her how to live without the constant expectation of pain.
